title: What the 'nanometer' in a phone chip really means
description: Chip nodes like 5nm or 3nm used to be real measurements. Today they work more like generation names.

scenes.big: The 'nm' number is now a label
scenes.say: Your phone's chip is labeled with a size in nanometers. That number doesn't mean what you'd expect.
Decades ago, the node name was a real measurement. A 0.35 micron node had gates about 0.35 microns long. But by Intel's 130 nanometer chips, the gate was already 70. At 22 nanometers, it was 35.

New transistor shapes changed performance without tracking the name. Intel's Mark Bohr said some dimensions are smaller than the node name, and others are larger. One foundry's 14 nanometer chips used the same wiring density as its 20.
Researchers have noted that the label is decoupled from the real gate length, so one company's number isn't directly comparable to another's.
Better things to compare are transistor density, performance per watt, and real-world results. Follow for more chip talk.
